title: Riggs v. Palmer (1889)
summary: A statute’s general words yield to the evident intention of its makers and to the common-law maxim that no one may profit from his own wrong, so a grandson who murdered the testator to secure his inheritance cannot take under a will that the wills statutes, read literally, would give effect to.
notes: Court of Appeals of New York, 1889. Key line: No one shall be permitted to profit by his own fraud, or to take advantage of his own wrong, or to found any claim upon his own iniquity, or to acquire property by his own crime. (Judge Earl)

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs and appellants were Philo Riggs, as guardian ad litem, and Francis B. Palmer’s two daughters, Mrs. Riggs and Mrs. Preston, who received small legacies under the will and sought to keep the estate from passing to the murderer. The defendants and respondents were Elmer E. Palmer, the testator’s sixteen-year-old grandson and residuary legatee, and the estate’s administrator; Elmer claimed the property under a formally valid, probated will. Judge Earl wrote for the Court of Appeals of New York on October 8, 1889; Judge Gray dissented.
sections.Material Facts: On August 13, 1880 Francis Palmer made a will leaving small legacies to his daughters and the residue of his farm and considerable personal property to his grandson Elmer, subject to support for Elmer’s mother. Francis later married Mrs. Bresee under an antenuptial agreement charging her support against the farm. Elmer lived in his grandfather’s household, knew of the provisions in his favor, and knew that Francis had shown an intention to revoke them. To prevent revocation and obtain immediate possession, Elmer willfully poisoned his grandfather in 1882. He was convicted of second-degree murder and was serving his sentence in the state reformatory when this civil action began. The statutes governing the making, proof, effect and revocation of wills contained no provision disqualifying a beneficiary who murders the testator; read literally, they gave the residue to Elmer.
sections.Procedural History: The daughters sued to cancel and annul the provisions of the will in Elmer’s favor. A referee found that Elmer intentionally murdered Francis to prevent revocation of the will and accelerate his inheritance, yet concluded that the wills statutes required dismissal of the complaint; judgment was entered on the report and the General Term affirmed. On the daughters’ appeal the Court of Appeals accepted the facts found, reversed both judgments, and entered judgment enjoining Elmer and the administrator from using the estate for Elmer’s benefit, declaring the devise and bequest to him ineffective, and declaring the daughters owners of the estate subject to the support charges for Elmer’s mother and Francis’s widow.
sections.Issue: May a beneficiary acquire property under a formally valid and probated will after intentionally murdering the testator to prevent revocation and accelerate the inheritance, when the governing statutes contain no express slayer provision and, read literally, transfer the estate to him? Or may a court restrain a statute’s general words by the evident intention of the legislature and fundamental maxims of the common law?
sections.Holding: Elmer cannot take any interest in the estate. The wills statutes were enacted to carry out testators’ wishes and secure the orderly devolution of property, and a legislature pursuing those ends would never have intended a legatee who murdered the testator to benefit under the will; a case within the letter of a statute is not within the statute unless it is within the intention of its makers. Independently, all statutes and contracts are controlled by the maxim that no one shall profit by his own fraud, take advantage of his own wrong, or acquire property by his own crime. The ruling takes no property Elmer possessed and adds no punishment; it holds only that he shall not acquire property by his crime. Reversed, with judgment for the daughters.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Earl reasoned from legislative purpose, the equity of the statute and the absurdity doctrine. He conceded that the statutes, literally read, gave the property to the murderer, but held that their purpose controlled: what is within the makers’ intention is within the statute though outside its letter, and what is within the letter is outside the statute if outside the intention. Blackstone’s examples supplied the method: a law letting a man try all causes in his manor does not reach his own case. Common-law maxims against profiting from one’s own wrong were a second, independent ground, background law that governs statutes and wills unless legislation displaces it. The causal link made the maxim decisive: Francis might have revoked, and by killing him Elmer made the will speak at the time he chose. Judge Gray’s dissent applied a strictly textual method: the legislature had regulated wills with comprehensive particularity; the civil-law slayer rules supplied reasons for legislation, not judicial power, and stripping Elmer of the legacy added a penalty beyond his sentence.

topics.lrs-k-purposivism: Earl reads the wills statutes by the purpose of their makers and asks what the legislature would have said had the case been put to it, extending or restraining the words to match that intention.
topics.lrs-k-absurdity: The majority relies on Blackstone's rule that a statute's general words do not reach collateral consequences manifestly contradictory to common reason, illustrated by the manor of Dale and the Bologna barber.
topics.lrs-k-textualism: Gray's dissent holds the court to the letter of a statute that regulates wills 'with comprehensive particularity' and treats the missing exception as a matter for the legislature alone.
topics.lrs-k-canons: The opinion states the canon that a thing within the intention of the makers is within the statute though not within the letter, and applies common-law maxims against profiting from one's own wrong as background rules.
topics.lrs-k-lawmaking: Earl explains the gap by the drafting condition that lawmakers 'could not set down every case in express terms,' while Gray reads the same silence as a deliberate and complete legislative scheme.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Earl wrote for the majority. Judge Gray dissented, arguing that the court was bound by the 'rigid rules of law' enacted by the legislature, that a will validly executed and never revoked in a statutory mode must stand, that public policy was satisfied by punishing the crime, and that stripping Elmer of the legacy would impose an additional punishment and divert the estate to persons the testator may never have chosen.
learning.why: Riggs is the foundational contest between purposivism and textualism: Earl reads a statute by the intention of its makers, the equity of the statute and the absurdity doctrine, while Gray insists that a comprehensive statutory scheme leaves no room for judicial correction. It also shows a court using common-law maxims to control statutory language.
